content: Suet is the raw fat derived from beef or mutton, particularly the dense fat located around the loins and kidneys. It has a melting point between 45°C and 50°C (113°F to 122°F) and solidifies at temperatures between 37°C and 40°C (98.6°F to 104°F). The primary application of suet is in the production of tallow, although it is also utilized as an ingredient in cooking. The process of rendering suet into tallow involves melting the fat, simmering it for an extended period, straining it, cooling it, and often repeating the entire process. Unlike suet, tallow can be stored for long durations without refrigeration. Tallow has various uses, including soap production, cooking (especially for frying), as bird feed, and historically, for making candles. Suet is a critical component in preparing the pastry for steamed steak and kidney pudding. In this dish, suet crust pastry is used to line a pudding bowl, with the meat placed inside and sealed with a lid of suet crust pastry. The pudding is then steamed for approximately four hours before serving. Suet pastry is soft in texture, contrasting with the crispness of shortcrust pastry. Its low melting point allows it to remain solid at room temperature but melt easily under moderate heat, such as during steaming. It is important to distinguish suet from beef dripping, which is the fat and juices collected from a roasting pan during the preparation of roast beef. Unlike suet, beef dripping is not rendered. As suet is derived from the fat surrounding the kidneys, it requires the removal of connective tissue, blood, and other non-fat components. It is then coarsely grated to make it ready for use. Fresh suet must be refrigerated and consumed within a few days of purchase, similar to other meat products. Packaged suet available in supermarkets is typically dehydrated and mixed with flour to ensure stability at room temperature. However, the addition of flour may necessitate adjustments when using it in older recipes that call for fresh suet, as the fat-to-flour ratio can differ. Most modern recipes specify the use of packaged suet. Vegetarian suet substitutes are also available in UK supermarkets. These are made from fats such as palm oil combined with rice flour. They resemble shredded beef suet and can be used as a substitute in recipes, though the results may differ slightly from those achieved with animal-derived suet. Suet-based bird feeders are particularly favored by various bird species, including woodpeckers, goldfinches, juncos, cardinals, thrushes, jays, kinglets, bluebirds, wrens, and starlings.
